title: Med Spa Failed Membership Payments: A Past-Due Playbook (November 2026)
summary: Med spa failed membership payments: how to set retries, a grace period, member messages and a past-due list so declined cards stop turning into cancellations.
body_markdown:
## Why Memberships Fail Without Anyone Deciding to Cancel


A membership payment fails for a reason the member usually does not know about: the card expired, the bank flagged a recurring charge, a new card replaced a lost one, or the balance was short on the billing date. The member did not choose to leave, which is why this loss is called involuntary churn.


The cost builds quietly. A clinic that bills 200 members and loses 3 percent of charges to declines each month has 6 members a month sliding toward a lapse they never asked for. Support conversations with clinic operators show how it plays out: the owner finds out a member is behind only when the member books, and by then the history is hard to untangle. One clinic told us that before it had a single past-due view, someone had to open each membership to see who was late.


The fix is not a harsher policy. It is a process that makes the decline visible the day it happens and gives the member an easy way to fix it.


## What a Retry Schedule Should Look Like


A good retry schedule tries the card several times over one to two weeks instead of once or every day. Spacing attempts gives temporary holds and short balances time to clear, and it keeps you from stacking up declines on a card that the bank is already watching.


Published defaults are a useful anchor. Stripe's documentation recommends its Smart Retries setting of[8 tries within 2 weeks](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/smart-retries) , and its custom schedule allows up to three retries, each a set number of days after the last. Those are processor settings, so confirm what your own payment processor and software actually do before you promise members a timeline.


Day Action Who does it


0 Charge fails; member is flagged past due Software


1 First text and email with a card-update link Software or front desk


3-4 Second automatic retry Software


7 Second message, friendlier and more specific about the date benefits pause Front desk


10-14 Final retry, then a personal call for higher-value members Front desk


After grace period Benefits pause; membership stays on file Policy


Not every decline deserves a retry. A card reported lost or stolen, or one the issuer permanently rejects, will not succeed on a second try. Stripe lists these as[hard decline codes](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/smart-retries#hard-decline-codes) that only clear once the member provides a new payment method. For those, skip the waiting and go straight to the message.


## Setting a Grace Period Members Will Accept


A grace period of seven to fourteen days works for most clinics. It is long enough to cover a reissued card or a payday, and short enough that a member cannot collect several months of benefits on an unpaid plan.


Decide three things and write them down:


- **What stays active during the grace period.** Most operators keep everything active, since a member who just forgot to update a card should not be locked out mid-week.
- **What pauses afterward.** Member pricing on new bookings and credit redemption are the usual first two.
- **What ends the membership.** Many agreements allow termination after 30 days unpaid, and the clinic keeps any prepaid credits visible on the books so nothing is lost in the move.


Apply the rule the same way every time. The exception you grant a friendly regular is the one the next member will quote back at you. If you also bill by[packages and prepaid credits](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-package-refund-policy) , state separately what happens to a balance when a payment lapses.


## The Messages That Get a Card Updated


The best past-due message is short, specific and makes the fix a single tap. Lead with the fact that the payment did not go through, name the amount and the membership, and put the update link in the first two lines.


A first text can be as plain as: "Hi, your monthly membership payment didn't go through. You can update your card here in under a minute. Your benefits stay active until the 14th." The second message, a week in, adds the date benefits pause and offers a phone number. Skip legal language and avoid words like "delinquent" in anything the member sees; guides to dunning, including[Checkout Page's dunning glossary](https://checkoutpage.com/glossary/dunning) , recommend subject lines framed as a card update request.


Two guardrails apply. First, the member must have agreed to texts from you, and billing messages should be covered by that consent, as laid out in our guide to[text message consent](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-text-message-consent) . Second, keep treatment details out of the message entirely. A text that says "your Botox membership" is a patient disclosure sitting on a lock screen, so say "your membership" and stop there.


## Working Past-Due Membership Payments From One List Each Week


A weekly past-due list is the habit that recovers the most revenue, because it replaces memory with a queue. One person owns it, opens it on a set day, and works from the oldest balance down.


A ten-minute routine looks like this:


1. Open every membership that is past due, sorted by how long it has been unpaid.
2. For anyone inside the grace period, confirm the automatic message went out.
3. For anyone at day seven or beyond, send a payment link by text or email, or call if the plan is a high tier.
4. Record what happened: updated card, asked to pause, asked to cancel, no response.
5. Move anyone past the grace period to the pause state your policy describes.


The payoff shows up fast. One clinic reported collecting $700 in a single afternoon the first time its team worked a consolidated past-due report, money that had been sitting in individual patient files. That is an anecdote and not a benchmark, but it matches what operators describe: the revenue was never gone, it was just invisible.


## Payment Plans, Cancellation Fees and Other Charges That Fail Differently


Membership renewals are not the only scheduled charge that can fail, and each type follows its own rules. A payment plan for a high-ticket treatment, a deposit and a cancellation fee should each have a written answer to "does this charge on its own, or does someone have to push it through?"


This question comes up in support conversations more than any other billing topic. An owner sees a scheduled installment on a patient's record and asks whether it will withdraw automatically, because the cancellation fees she expected to collect on their own did not. In many systems cancellation and no-show fees are a separate setting from scheduled installments, so one can be automatic while the other is manual. Check each setting individually and test it with a small charge.


Charge type Usually automatic? What to confirm


Monthly membership renewal Yes, on the billing date Retry schedule and card-update message


Payment plan installment Yes, against the saved card That a card is saved and still valid before the due date


Cancellation or no-show fee Depends on a setting Whether auto-collect is on, covered in our guide to[reducing no-shows](https://decodahealth.com/blog/how-to-reduce-med-spa-no-shows)


Deposit at booking Charged at booking Refund rule if the patient cancels


Also ask what time of day the batch runs. Renewals usually process in a daily batch, not at a promised minute, so tell members "on the 1st" and not "at 6 a.m." If a member asks mid-morning whether the charge has gone through, the honest answer is that the day's batch is still running.


## Staying on the Right Side of Recurring-Billing Rules


Recurring charges carry disclosure and cancellation rules, and a past-due process has to respect them. The FTC enforces clear disclosure of material terms and easy cancellation under the[Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/statutes/restore-online-shoppers-confidence-act) , and that enforcement has continued, as this[Holland & Knight summary of subscription enforcement](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/09/ftc-steps-up-subscription-enforcement-after-click-to-cancel-rule) explains.


In practice that means three habits. Put your retry and grace-period rules in the membership agreement the member signed. Keep the cancel path as easy as the signup path, including for a member who is behind. And never keep charging a member who has asked to cancel because a past-due sequence was still running, so exclude anyone in an active cancellation request from reminders. State laws add more, such as the California rules summarized in this[Kilpatrick Townsend alert](https://ktslaw.com/en/Insights/Alert/2024/10/California-Latest-Automatic-Renewal-Law-Amendments-Take-Effect-in-July-2025) , and our overview of[new med spa laws](https://decodahealth.com/blog/new-med-spa-laws) tracks the ones to watch. Have a healthcare or consumer attorney review the final wording.


## Questions to Ask Your Software About Declined Payments


Before you rely on any billing system, ask how it behaves on a bad day and have it show you. Operators who switch platforms often discover the answers only after a month of silent declines.


- Where do I see every past-due member in one place, and can I sort by days overdue?
- Does the system retry automatically, and can I change the schedule?
- Can I send a payment link by text or email straight from that list?
- When I recover an overdue payment, does the member's next billing date move?
- Can a member update their own card without calling the front desk?


The billing-date question matters most. Recovering a missed month can shift the cycle or bill two periods at once in some systems, a trap we described in our guide to[raising membership prices on existing members](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-price-increase) . Test one account through a decline and a recovery before you trust it with everyone.

## Measuring Whether the Process Works


Track three numbers each month: the share of renewal charges that fail, the share of failures recovered within the grace period, and the dollars lost to members who lapsed without choosing to. If the first is high, look at card-update prompts at signup. If the second is low, your messages or timing need work.


Separate involuntary lapses from real cancellations in your reports, since they need different fixes. The first is a billing process problem, while the second is a[retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) problem. Folding both into one churn number hides which lever to pull, and it makes[seasonal cash flow](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-seasonal-cash-flow-planning) harder to forecast.


## Final Thoughts on Recovering Past-Due Memberships


Declined cards cost clinics members who never meant to leave, and a written retry rule, a grace period and a weekly list are enough to recover most of them. Start this week by writing your grace period into the agreement and opening your current past-due list for the first time. ## Frequently Asked Questions


What should a med spa do when a membership payment fails?


Retry the charge automatically a few times over one to two weeks, message the member after the first failure with a link to update their card, and decide in advance whether benefits stay active during that window. Most declines are expired cards or temporary holds, so a calm text usually fixes them before a front-desk call is needed.


How long should a grace period be for a past-due med spa membership?


Seven to fourteen days is a common range, long enough to cover a card reissue or a payday and short enough that members cannot use several unpaid months of benefits. Write the number into the membership agreement, and apply it the same way to every member so the front desk never has to improvise.


Should a med spa pause membership benefits when a payment fails?


Pausing discounted booking and credit redemption once the grace period ends is the most common rule, because it protects you from giving away services on an unpaid plan. Keep benefits active during the grace period itself. Whatever you choose, tell members at signup so a pause never feels like a surprise penalty.


How many times should you retry a failed membership charge?


Payment processors that publish defaults land in the same range. Stripe's recommended Smart Retries setting is eight tries within two weeks, and its custom schedules allow up to three retries. Spacing attempts over days rather than hours avoids hammering a card and gives temporary holds time to clear.


Can a med spa text a member about an overdue membership payment?


Yes, if the member agreed to receive texts from you and the message is about their own account. Keep it short, ask them to update their card, and never include treatment details. Your text consent language should cover billing messages, so confirm it does before you build the sequence.


What is the difference between a failed payment and a cancelled membership?


A failed payment is a charge that did not go through, while a cancellation is a decision by the member or by your policy. Treating them as the same thing is how clinics lose members who never meant to leave. Track involuntary lapses separately so you can see how much revenue is slipping through billing and not through choice.
